question: In recent years, the European Commission has taken many steps to better protect children’s rights online. Although there appear to be sufficient legal frameworks in place to address the known challenges, these policy initiatives have had less of an impact that one would have hoped1.

Analyses and reports by the European Commission show that certain legal frameworks are in need of a ‘digital update’, that existing legislation is not being adequately enforced and that international cooperation on law enforcement is insufficiently effective.

The Commission is taking steps – the recent guidelines on the Digital Services Act are one such example – but the protection of children online is fragmented across various legal frameworks and requires coordinated legal action across Member State borders and even legal frameworks. The following questions arise in this regard: 1.
How will trusted flaggers be financially supported in view of their increased workload?

How will digital services coordinators be encouraged to run campaigns to encourage children/young people to report more, and how will the Commission ensure strong cooperation between the various national supervisory authorities and more cross-border legal action?
Will guidelines be drawn up for the risk assessments referred to in Article 34 of the regulation, and what industry standards will be developed for age verification and age estimation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.11.2025) Trusted flagger activities under the Digital Services Act1 (DSA) require adequate support. The Commission is now preparing the Guidelines on trusted flaggers, and Member States and Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) are encouraged to provide capacity building and resources to trusted flaggers.

The proposed Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) 2028-20342 retains support for civil society organisations as a priority. The new AgoraEU programme will build on current programmes3 with an increased indicative budget of almost EUR 9 billion, strengthening democracy, providing support to media and civil society.

Safer Internet Centres4 run campaigns, produce educational material, and organise events about the protection of minors online. They also offer helplines for advice on harmful content and hotlines to report illegal content. Through the European Board for Digital Services, DSCs meet to ensure consistent enforcement and cross-border cooperation.

The working group on protection of minors is coordinating enforcement actions targeting pornographic platforms5 and actions to ensure compliance by smaller platforms with the DSA and the Guidelines on the protection of minors6.

The Commission, in cooperation with the DSCs, may issue guidelines to present best practices and recommend possible measures for relevant providers to comply with obligations to mitigate systemic risks. To support an EU-wide age verification system, the Commission is developing a common approach with Member States and industry.

In July, the Commission released an Age Verification Blueprint7 defining technical specifications considered a reference standard by the protection of minors guidelines, and a white-label app that Member States and other entities can further customise.
